new_statements.quote: § 71. The primitive Germanic language developed a stress accent which fell upon the first syllable of all words, and this is in essentials preserved in all the Germanic languages. Thus in Old English we find the stress on the first syllable in all simple words, and in most compound words: [word, stānas, lufiende, sīþfæt, andgiet, andwyrde, unnytt, onsæge — accent marks garbled in the scanned]. § 72. The main exception to this rule is due to the fact that in Germanic a syntactic combination of prepositional adverb with verb was not yet a single word at the time when the main stress of words was fixed on the first syllable, and such combinations ultimately developed into compound words stressed on the second element.

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the catalog record (StressTyp2 initial stress = initial stress). Campbell adds the principled exceptions (unstressed verbal prefixes incl. ge-, prefixed compound adverbs) and a weight-conditioned half-stress system.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Main stress on the first syllable of every simple word and of most compounds (noun/adjective compounds stressed on the first element). Exception: verbs compounded with a prepositional-adverb prefix (āþencan, oþflēon, wiþsacan) are stressed on the second element; the prefix ge- is always unstressed (§74); nouns derived from such verbs keep the unstressed prefix (forgifness), while verbs derived from compound nouns keep initial stress (andwyrdan) (§77).
new_statements.secondary_stress: §§87-92 (pp. 34-35): a half-stress falls on the second element of a compound when both elements keep full meaning (goldwlanc); second elements with reduced meaning and heavy derivative suffixes (-els, -end, -ere, -ing, -ung, -ness, -isc, etc.) carry half-stress only after a long syllable or its equivalent when an unaccented syllable follows (æþelinges, singende have it; cyninges, wesende do not) — a weight-conditioned secondary stress; any long final syllable after a long syllable acquires half-stress when an inflexion is added (Hengestes).
new_statements.exceptions: Prepositional-adverb + verb compounds stressed on the second element (§72); ge- always unstressed (§74); compound adverbs with a prepositional first element stressed on the second element, e.g. todæg, onweg, beforan (§82); most adverb+adverb compounds stressed on the second (þā-gēn) but nū-þā on the first (§84); þǣr+preposition stressed on the preposition (§85); full- subordinated, eall- stressed (§86); participles mostly take verbal stress (§81); verbs are more lightly stressed than nouns in the sentence (§93).
new_statements.identity_note: Both opened works describe Old English as a whole (West Saxon, Kentish, Anglian forms cited side by side); no single dialect is singled out for the stress rule. Campbell notes Anglian (Vespasian Psalter, Kentish Glosses) survivals of the prefix ot- but the stress statement is general.

new_statements.quote: § 10. The rule for the accentuation of uncompounded words is the same in Old English as in the oldest period of the other Germanic languages, viz. the chief stress fell upon the stem-syllable and always remained there even when suffixes and inflexional endings followed it, as beran, to bear; dagas, days. [...] The position of the secondary stress in trisyllabic and polysyllabic words fluctuated in OE., and with the present state of our knowledge of the subject it is impossible to formulate any hard and fast rules concerning it.

new_statements.relation_note: Agrees with the catalog's initial-stress record for simplex words and noun/adjective compounds; formulates it as stem-syllable stress and adds the unstressed-prefix exceptions and secondary-stress remarks. It could also be labelled morphologically determined (stem-syllable), which for Old English coincides with initial stress except after unstressed prefixes.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Chief stress on the stem syllable of uncompounded words, i.e. the first syllable, and it stays there regardless of suffixes or inflexions (beran, dagas, æþelingas, huntigestre). Compounds whose second element is a noun or adjective are stressed on the first syllable (§11, p. 15: āctrēam-type, brȳdguma); words formed with an inseparable particle or with ge- have the chief stress on the second element (§12, p. 16: bebod, forbod, gebed); compound verbs are stressed on the second element if the prefix is inseparable (becuman, forgiefan) and on the first if separable (æfterfolgian, ūtdrīfan) (§14, pp. 16-17).
new_statements.secondary_stress: §10, p. 14: position of secondary stress in trisyllabic and polysyllabic words 'fluctuated in OE.' and no hard-and-fast rules can be given. §13, p. 16: in compound nouns the chief secondary stress falls on the syllable of the second element that would bear chief stress alone (brȳdguma, fēowergield); compounds no longer felt as such lose the strong secondary stress (ēorod, hlāford, werod). §16, p. 17: compound adverbs stress the more important element (eal(l)mǣst, ealneg, ealswā vs onweg, tōgædere, þǣrinne).
new_statements.exceptions: Inseparable verbal prefixes and ge- take no chief stress, so bebod, gebed, becuman, forgiefan are stressed on the second element (§§12, 14); verbs formed from compound nouns (andswarian, andwyrdan, fultumian) keep initial stress (§14); nouns formed directly from prefixed verbs (onginn, ongietennes) keep second-element stress (§11).
new_statements.identity_note: Both opened works describe Old English as a whole (West Saxon, Kentish, Anglian forms cited side by side); no single dialect is singled out for the stress rule. Campbell notes Anglian (Vespasian Psalter, Kentish Glosses) survivals of the prefix ot- but the stress statement is general.

new_statements.quote: 2.84 OE had, like PDE, a stress-based system of accentuation, and in this respect differed from late IE, where a pitch-based system of accentuation existed, see §3.4. Furthermore, in OE, as elsewhere in Gmc, stress soon came to be fixed upon the first syllable of a word, that is to say, OE developed a ‘left-strong’ stress system. [...] 2.87 No problems are presented by words with only one root morpheme, where the first syllable is always stressed, for example, wórd ‘word’, .fel [= ýfel] ‘evil’, wrlon [= wréon] ‘cover’. In such words the addition of an inflexional syllable has no effect, for example, wórdes gen.sg.

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the catalog record (fixed-strict initial; Wright & Wright §10 'chief stress fell upon the stem-syllable', Campbell 1959 §71 'stress on the first syllable in all simple words') and the same main exception (unstressed verbal prefixes, Campbell §72): Hogg §2.84/§2.87 'fixed upon the first syllable of a word.. the first syllable is always stressed'. Adds detail not on record: weight-conditioned, left-to-right secondary stress (§2.86-2.87, only non-final heavy syllables; light initial syllables still primary-stressed), the stressed-nominal vs unstressed-verbal prefix minimal pairs (§2.88), suffix/name second elements (§§2.89-90) and the exception classes of §2.91 (compound adve…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Old English has stress accent fixed on the first syllable of the word ('left-strong'): in words with one root morpheme the first syllable always carries primary stress and inflexional endings never move it (wórd, wórdes). §2.86: stress is assigned left to right; only heavy syllables can bear stress except the initial syllable, which may be stressed even if light when an unstressed syllable follows; the leftmost stressed syllable gets primary stress, all other stressed syllables secondary. Stress-bearing elements: lexical roots, prefixes of nouns/adjectives, historically free derivational suffixes, second elements of names. §2.88: nominal/adjectival prefixes are stressed (ándgit, órleahtre) but inseparable verbal prefixes are unstressed proclitics, so prefixed verbs stress the root (forbérnan, ofercúman), giving noun/verb minimal pairs (ǽfþanca : ofþýncan, ándsaca : onsácan..); compounds: primary stress on the first element, secondary on the second.
new_statements.secondary_stress: §2.86-2.87: a non-initial heavy syllable of the root bears secondary stress only if it is not word-final, so inflexion changes the pattern (ǽþeling but ǽþelìngas; cyningas has none because the first syllable is light, n.1); second elements of compounds carry secondary stress (stǽfcræ̀ft, gámolfèax, híldfrùma); §2.89 suffixes from free morphemes (-dōm, -hād, -lēas, -līc, -scipe..) bear secondary stress only when disyllabic by origin or inflexion, else lose stress with vowel shortening (cynedom); §2.90 same for second elements of names (Hrōþgār vs Hrōþgāres); §2.85 -līc(e) secondary-stressed after lexical bases (gelustfullīce) but unstressed after non-lexical ones (hwelc). Sievers's double primary stress in compounds is rejected (§2.87 n.2).
new_statements.exceptions: §2.91: (1) compound adverbs of preposition + noun/adverb are stressed on the SECOND element (todǽg, onbǽc, befóran, begeóndan; reduced bæftan, bútan, búfan, bínnan; fullóft); þā/þǣr unstressed in nūþā, þāgīt, þǣrinne; eall- stressed (éallswā, éalneg). (2) prefix variation from the noun/verb contrast: (a) deverbal nouns keep the unstressed prefix (forgífness, ālýsing, bebód, behát, forbód; but bíspell, fórwyrd), (b) denominal verbs keep the stressed prefix (ándswarian, fúltumian, ándwyrdan), (c) participles usually follow the verb (underþéoded, occasionally únderþeoded), (d) un- normally primary-stressed (únclǣne) but sometimes shifted to the root (unclǽne), (e) ge- never stressed (gescéaft, gelíc). Separable verbal prefixes (æfter, fore, inn, ofer..) are stressed like compound first elements when attached (ínngangan, ǽfterspyrian).
new_statements.identity_note: Hogg 1992 vol. 1 treats Old English of c.425-c.1125 across dialects (West Saxon, Kentish, Mercian, Northumbrian per ch. 1 §§1.5-1.12); the excerpt read is the general introduction only.

audit.action: a better source should be cited for the same classification
audit.reasoning: (1) Deciding quotation confirmed verbatim in the held Wright & Wright 1914 djvu text at pp. 15-16 §10, with §§11-14 as cited; held Sweet 1905 corroborates. (2) Deciding source is a genuine (if, 1914) historical-comparative reference grammar with an Accentuation section, not a pedagogical primer; the better-ranked Glottolog grammars (Campbell 1959, Hogg 1992/2011) are not yet obtained and not open, but OE root-initial primary stress with unstressed ge-/be-/for- and verbal prefixes is stated identically in every source opened. (3) downloaded the open-access Fulk 2014 Introductory Grammar (ACMRS; IU ScholarWorks) to; §22 pp. 14-15 confirms the classification (fixed initial/root stress, strict, prefix exceptions morphological).

sources.quote: '22. Most words are accented on the first syllable. There are two exceptions: (1) the prefix ge- is never stressed, and the prefixes be- and for- almost never; (2) prefixes of verbs are unstressed, so that the primary stress falls on the root syllable, as in aþencan, underwreðian, ætspornan (cf. ǽtspornung). When a verb is stressed on the prefix (and this is rare), as in andswarian, it is because the verb is derived from a noun... Even names taken from Latin sources are almost always stressed on the first syllable.' §23: 'A half-stress falls on some middle and final syllables...'
